content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes CLR-GAM, which is an unsupervised representation learning method for point clouds. Build upon vanilia contrastive learning, CLR-GAM consists of two more parts: Guided Augmentation (GA) and Guided Feature Mapping (GFM). For each training step, GA selects the most “rarely” used augmentation in the previous training steps from a number of randomly sampled augmentations; the method use GFM to undo the augmentation in the first view and files the closest point feature (in original Euclidean 3D space) to compute InfoNCE loss. The authors show the good performance of CLR-GAM on 3D point cloud classification, few-shot learning, and object part segmentation tasks on object-level point cloud datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

- The paper is well-written and easy to understand.
- The experiment setups are explained clearly and the code is provided.
- The authors show good performance of the proposed method on three downstream tasks on object-level point cloud datasets.

Weakness:

- The proposed Guided Feature Mapping (GFM) is actually very similar to PointContrast [1] and its follow-up papers [2]. GFM undoes the augmentation in view 1 and applies the augmentation for view 2 to find the correspondence of between points in view 1 and view 2. (If I understand correctly, this step can actually be skipped by first establishing identity correspondence before all augmentations of the two views, and maintaining such correspondence while doing the augmentation.) With this, infoNCE loss is applied to point features rather than object-level features. It seems to me this is very similar to what PointContrast does, and I did not find where this is discussed/compared in the paper. (Btw, in the related work section, PointContrast seems to be categorized into “All these methods rely on contrastive learning of encoded global features of point clouds, ignoring the structural deformations that lead to intra-class confusion.”, which is not true.)
- Only evaluate on object-level datasets. At the beginning of the introduction, the authors emphasize “scene understanding” in 3D, but most of the main experiments are conducted on object-level datasets (ModelNet-40, ShapeNet, ScanNet). While similar methods (e.g. PointContrast) conduct extensive experiments on scene-level point cloud datasets (SUN-RGBD, ScanNet, etc.) for more complex tasks (3D object detection, segmentation). I would suggest the authors also compare with relevant methods on scene-level point cloud datasets to support the paper better.

Minor:

- I am a bit confused by the distance function for the rotations in GA: does the sum mean summing over the xyz Euler angles? and where does the 0.5 come from? Plus, could the authors provide more details about how to set \alpha_R, \alpha_T, and \alpha_S?
- Table 3 is a bit confusing at first glance: there are four columns in the lower row (PNet, DGCNN, PNet, DGCNN), and I guess they correspond to 10-shot and 5-shot respectively? I would suggest either turning this table into two tables or adding a row to explain this. And I would suggest keeping more space between the caption of table 3 and the main text.

[1] Saining Xie, Jiatao Gu, Demi Guo, Charles R Qi, Leonidas Guibas, and Or Litany. Pointcontrast: Unsupervised pre-training for 3d point cloud understanding. In European conference on computer vision, pp. 574–591. Springer, 2020.
[2] Hou, Ji, et al. Exploring data-efficient 3d scene understanding with contrastive scene contexts. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2021.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: Good. This paper is well-written and easy to understand.

Quality: Fair. The experiments on object-level datasets are quite clear, and ablation is good. I think it is necessary to compare with other methods on scene-level datasets.

Novelty: Fair. In my view, GFM is very similar to PointContrast.

Reproducibility: Good. The code and pre-trained models are provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I think the proposed method makes sense and the evaluation on the object-level dataset is good. But I am mostly concerned about the limited novelty (GFM is actually not new) and no evaluation on the scene-level datasets.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new contrastive learning-based framework for 3D point cloud. The framework address two main issues of example ambiguity and augmentation space coverage. To do that they propose guided feature mapping and guided augmentations and show their effectiveness in object classification, few-shot learning, and part segmentation. The paper also includes an ablation study and supplemental material which include additional results and trained models and code for reproducibility.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

Usefulness: Self-supervised frameworks for point clouds are an interesting and active field of research and this paper takes on this important task. 

Evaluation: It shows that the authors went to great lengths to support their claim of SOTA performance on multiple tasks. Few-Shot learning performance looks promising. Performance are even comparable to methods that use an additional modality. Furthermore, the supplemental materials contain additional results. 

Writing: The paper was overall well-written and easy to follow. all mathematical notations are explicitly provided, and while a bit not standard or confusing at times, helped me understand the paper. 

Weaknesses:

Novelty: The novelty of the approach is unclear to me. Applying predetermined transformations on synthetic point clouds is not new. The augmentation space exploration highly relies on previous work (Badia et. al.) and the point cloud back-bones are well established without any noticeable alterations. 

Related work: The work reports performance on point cloud classification but did not address some issues raised in "Revisiting point cloud shape classification with a simple and effective baseline" by Goyal et.al. This has bearings on the classification evaluation performance which are marginal.

Evaluation: Improvement compared to the previous SOTA is minor for classification and part segmentation.
The t-SNE plot shows that better clustering is obtained only in one or two classes which raises a question of the generalizability of the approach and the quality of the learned features. Further discussion on this matter is missing in the paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The paper is well-written and easy to follow. Figures are good and help understand the better with a generally good flow of the story and idea (despite some repetitions). 

Quality: The quality of the paper is good overall. All claims are supported by experiments and an ablation study is done to explore different aspects of the approach. It seems that the paper tries to avoid discussing some shortcomings (see weaknesses above about marginal improvements and learned feature generalizability). 

Novelty: This is where the paper falls a bit short. While the paper has shown well how it is useful in an abundance of experiments, it is not clear to me how original it is. 

Reproducibility: Code and models are available in the supplementary material.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is well-written and easy to follow. The proposed approach is generally interesting, but the novelty is not clear at this stage. However, the evaluation is very thorough and provides more than adequate support for the usefulness of the method, despite some minor shortcomings in the methodology and missing discussion in the ablation.

content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper the authors study contrastive learning on point clouds. Two key ideas are proposed in the CLR-GAM framework: the first is to use a memory bank to record used augmentations and encourage sampling novel data augmentations. The second is to transform point clouds before and after data augmentation into the same coordinate system and make sure that close points in the Euclidean space also have close features in the latent space. The authors claim that their method can achieve state-of-the-art performance on 3D object understanding tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- The paper is clearly written and the method is very easy to understand.
- The authors open source their code in the supplementary material to facilitate reproduction.

Technical Weaknesses:

- In general, all the experiments are conducted on tiny-scale datasets in this paper. In this case I don't feel that the conclusions in this paper (e.g. SOTA-level accuracy) is reliable. Papers in the same domain (e.g. PointContrast, ECCV'20 and DepthContrast, ICCV'21) generally proves that their methods can work on large-scale outdoor datasets. 
- Guided Feature Mapping really reminds me of PointContrast which is based on point cloud registration. The high-level idea is almost the same: PointContrast encourages registered point pairs to have similar features while in this paper the authors encourage closest points in the Euclidean space will have similar features. I feel that the authors did not discuss the related work PointContrast very extensively. 
- I think the method of this paper is tightly coupled with **object-level** contrastive learning. I'm not sure whether it is straightforward to generalize it to scene-level contrastive learning (which DepthContrast did). The cost for finding nearest neighbor pairs between two large-scale 3D scenes can be very expensive, and there might not be a concept of "class" in 3D scenes.

Non-technical Comments:
- (formatting) I would suggest the authors to embed all the text in the figures directly into the PDF instead of inserting PNGs to the document, just like what you did in Figures 1 and 2.
- Figure 1a is quite intuitive, but I did not quite get what Figure 1b is talking about. The authors might need to make it more intuitive in future revisions.
- It would be better if the authors can cite related work more extensively in the experiment section (e.g. supervised learning methods). E.g. at least you should include some results from PointCNN in Table 5, which is a very famous paper published 4 years ago with better results.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The paper writing is clear.
- The experiment quality and methodology is not satisfactory.
- The proposed method is not very novel compared with existing work.
- The paper should be reproducible (code is provided).
content.summary_of_the_review: The experiments in this paper are all limited to very small scale object datasets and the paper did not make an extensive comparison with PointContrast (ECCV'20) and DepthContrast (ICCV'21) on large-scale benchmarks. As such, I believe that this paper is clearly below the bar of ICLR 2023 in its current form.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Point cloud recognition has been a long-standing problem in computer vision and robotics. Compared to other data, point clouds are much harder to annotate. Therefore, learning from point clouds without annotations remains a challenging but useful problem. This paper studies self-supervised representation learning from point clouds, where the task is to learn representations/feature extractors by training with contrastive loss. However, due to the misalignment issue caused by data augmentations, simply applying contrastive loss damages the learned representations. So this paper proposes two data augmentation sampling strategies to stabilize contrastive learning, namely guided feature mapping (GFM) and guided augmentation (GA). GFM inverses a data augmentation in the feature space and matches the augmented point clouds with original point clouds to avoid feature misalignment. GA maintains a memory bank of data augmentations and samples diverse sets of data augmentations in each iteration. The proposed methods shows empirical improvements on several downstream applications such as point cloud classification and part segmentation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

1. This paper presents a clear motivation to study how to stabilize data augmentation strategy for point clouds.

2. This paper proposes two modules to improve point cloud data augmentation strategies. The proposed modules are technically sound and show some empirical improvements. 


Weaknesses:

1. My major concern is the novelty of the proposed modules. Although these modules were not formally discussed in other papers, they were already widely used in many works. For example, PointContrast also aligns features from different views of point clouds (w/ or w/o data augmentation), followed by contrastive loss in the feature space. Such operation is essentially GFM proposed in this paper. 

2. This paper introduces marginal empirical improvements compared to other methods. Since this paper doesn't claim using the same architectures/backbones with other methods, it's not clear that whether the comparison is fair.

3. Also, this paper doesn't talk about model details -- what are the concrete configurations of PointNet and DGCNN used in this paper? More ablation of model configurations should be done as well. 

4. Even this paper shows some improvements on several point cloud benchmarks, they are all synthetic data in a small regime. These benchmarks focus on either per-point or per-shape classification. A justification on realistic and large scale data is missing. This paper compares to PointContrast only on the ShapeNet-part experiment and ignore other settings that PointContrast has studied. It would be more convincing if this paper can demonstrate better performance on those tasks as well.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:

I think this paper clearly presents the motivation and ideas. I have no trouble following the presentation of this paper. 

Quality:

Quality is medium. A lot of model details and ablation studies are missing. Therefore, it's hard to justify the empirical value of this paper. 

Novelty:

Novelty is limited. The proposed modules have been already widely used in existing works though without being formally discussed. 

Reproducibility:

It's not easy to reproduce the paper based on current level of details.
content.summary_of_the_review: My recommendation is mainly based on the novelty and empirical value of this paper. Although this paper proposes two seemingly interesting modules, they have been already widely studied in prior works. Also, the empirical improvements introduced in this paper are very limited. Finally, some justifications on realistic data and ablation studies are needed.
